ketone: One of a large class of organic substances resembling the aldehydes, obtained by the distillation of certain salts of organic acids and consisting of carbonyl (CO) united with two hydrocarbon radicals. In general the ketones are colorless volatile liquids having a pungent ethereal odor.
kefirgrains: Small hard yellowish aggregations found in the Caucasus region, and containing various yeasts and bacteria. They are used as a ferment in preparing kefir.
kelp: 1. The calcined ashes of seaweed, -- formerly much used in the manufacture of glass, now used in the manufacture of iodine. 2. (Bot.) Any large blackish seaweed. Note: Laminaria is the common kelp of Great Britain; Macrocystis pyrifera and Nereocystis Lutkeana are the great kelps of the Pacific Ocean.
kerchered: Covered, or bound round, with a kercher. (old) G. Fletcher.
kettledrum: 1. (Mus.) A drum made of thin copper in the form of a hemispherical kettle, with parchment stretched over the mouth of it. Note: Kettledrums, in pairs, were formerly used in martial music for cavalry, but are now chiefly confined to orchestras, where they are called tympani. 2.
keratose: A tough, horny animal substance entering into the composition of the skeleton of sponges, and other invertebrates; -- called also keratode. | Containing hornlike fibers or fibers of keratose; belonging to the Keratosa.
kerf: A notch, channel, or slit made in any material by cutting or sawing.
kendal: A cloth colored green by dye obtained from the woad-waxen, formerly used by Flemish weavers at Kendal, in Westmoreland, England. J. Smith (Dict. Econ. Plants). How couldst thou know these men in Kendal green Shak.
kernel: 1. The essential part of a seed; all that is within the seed walls; the edible substance contained in the shell of a nut; hence, anything included in a shell, husk, or integument; | To harden or ripen into kernels; to produce kernels.
keloid: Applied to a variety of tumor forming hard, flat, irregular excrescences upon the skin. -- n. A keloid tumor.
keeled: 1. (Bot.) Keel-shaped; having a longitudinal prominence on the back; as, a keeled leaf. 2. (Zoöl.) Having a median ridge; carinate; as, a keeled scale.
keynote: 1. (Mus.) The tonic or first tone of the scale in which a piece or passage is written; the fundamental tone of the chord, to which all the modulations of the piece are referred; -- called also key tone. 2. The fundamental fact or idea; that which gives the key; as, the keynote of a policy or a sermon.
kennel: The water course of a street; a little canal or channel; a gutter; also, a puddle. Bp. Hall. | 1. A house for a dog or for dogs, or for a pack of hounds. A dog sure, if he could speak, had wit enough to describe his kennel. Sir P. Sidney. 2. A pack of hounds, or a collection of dogs. Shak. 3.
kevel: 1. (Naut.) A strong cleat to which large ropes are belayed. 2. A stone mason's hammer. [Written also cavil.] Kevel head (Naut.), a projecting end of a timber, used as a kevel.
kedge: To move (a vessel) by carrying out a kedge in a boat, dropping it overboard, and hauling the vessel up to it. | A small anchor used whenever a large one can be dispensed witch. See Kedge, v. t., and Anchor, n.
keyseat: To form a key seat, as by cutting. See Key seat, under Key.
keckle: To wind old rope around, as a cable, to preserve its surface from being fretted, or to wind iron chains around, to defend from the friction of a rocky bottom, or from the ice. Totten.
keeve: 1. (Brewing) A vat or tub in which the mash is made; a mash tub. Ure. 2. (Bleaching) A bleaching vat; a kier. 3. (Mining) A large vat used in dressing ores. | 1. To set in a keeve, or tub, for fermentation. 2. To heave; to tilt, as a cart. [Prov. Eng.]
kerchief: 1. A square of fine linen worn by women as a covering for the head; hence, anything similar in form or material, worn for ornament on other parts of the person; -- mostly used in compounds; as, neckerchief; breastkerchief; and later, handkerchief. He might put on a hat, a muffler, and a kerchief, and so escape. Shak.
kenspeckle: Having so marked an appearance as easily to be recognized. [Scot.]
ketch: An almost obsolete form of vessel, with a mainmast and a mizzenmast, -- usually from one hundred to two hundred and fifty tons burden. Bomb ketch. See under Bomb. | To catch. [Now obs. in spelling, and colloq. in pronunciation.] To ketch him at a vantage in his snares. Spenser.
kelpfish: A small California food fish (Heterostichus rostratus), living among kelp. The name is also applied to species of the genus Platyglossus.
keld: Having a kell or covering; webbed. (old) Drayton.
kendalgreen: A cloth colored green by dye obtained from the woad-waxen, formerly used by Flemish weavers at Kendal, in Westmoreland, England. J. Smith (Dict. Econ. Plants). How couldst thou know these men in Kendal green Shak.
keeper: 1. One who, or that which, keeps; one who, or that which, holds or has possession of anything. 2. One who retains in custody; one who has the care of a prison and the charge of prisoners. 3. One who has the care, custody, or superintendence of anything; as, the keeper of a park, a pound, of sheep, of a gate, etc. ; the keeper of attached property;
keen: 1. Sharp; having a fine edge or point; as, a keen razor, or a razor with a keen edge. A bow he bare and arwes [arrows] bright and kene. Chaucer. That my keen knife see not the wound it makes. Shak. | To sharpen; to make cold. Cold winter keens the brightening flood. Thomson.
keepership: The office or position of a keeper. Carew.
kerchiefed: Dressed; hooded; covered; wearing a kerchief. Milton.
kerana: A kind of long trumpet, used among the Persians. Moore (Encyc. of Music).
kersey: A kind of coarse, woolen cloth, usually ribbed, woven from wool of long staple.
keeler: 1. One employed in managing a Newcastle keel; -- called also keelman. 2. A small or shallow tub; esp., one used for holding materials for calking ships, or one used for washing dishes, etc.
kercher: A kerchief. (old) He became . . . white as a kercher. Sir T. North.
kenogenetic: Of or pertaining to kenogenesis; as, kenogenetic processes. -- Ken`o*ge*net"ic*al*ly, adv.
keelage: The right of demanding a duty or toll for a ship entering a port; also, the duty or toll. Bouvier. Wharton.
keener: A professional mourner who wails at a funeral. [Ireland]
kerse: A cress. (old) Chaucer. Not worth a kers. See under Cress.
keta: A small salmon (Oncorhynchus keta) of inferior value, which in the autumn runs up all the larger rivers between San Francisco and Kamchatka.
keystonestate: Pennsylvania; -- a nickname alluding to its having been the central one of the 13 original United States.
kentledge: Pigs of iron used for ballast. [Written also kintlidge.]
kestrel: A small, slender European hawk (Falco alaudarius), allied to the sparrow hawk. Its color is reddish fawn, streaked and spotted with white and black. Also called windhover and stannel. The name is also applied to other allied species. Note: This word is often used in contempt, as of a mean kind of hawk. "Kites and kestrels have a resemblance with hawks." Bacon.
kelt: Cloth with the nap, generally of native black wool. [Scot.] Jamieson. | A salmon after spawning. [Scot.]
keep: 1. To care; to desire. (old) I kepe not of armes for to yelp [boast]. Chaucer. 2. To hold; to restrain from departure or removal; not to let go of; to retain in one's power or possession; | 1. To remain in any position or state; to continue; to abide; to stay; as, to keep at a distance; to keep aloft; to keep near; to keep in the house; to keep before or behind; to keep in favor;
keno: A gambling game, a variety of the game of lotto, played with balls or knobs, numbered, and cards also numbered. [U. S.]
kemb: To comb. (old) His longe hair was kembed behind his back. Chaucer.
kerite: A compound in which tar or asphaltum combined with animal or vegetable oils is vulcanized by sulphur, the product closely resembling rubber; -- used principally as an insulating material in telegraphy. Knight.
keyboard: The whole arrangement, or one range, of the keys of an organ, typewriter, etc.
keepsake: Anything kept, or given to be kept, for the sake of the giver; a token of friendship.
kernish: Clownish; booorish. (old) "A petty kernish prince." Milton.
kern: 1. A light-armed foot soldier of the ancient militia of Ireland and Scotland; -- distinguished from gallowglass, and often used as a term of contempt. Macaulay. Now for our Irish wars; | A part of the face of a type which projects beyond the body, or shank.
kempty: Coarse, rough hair wool or fur, injuring its quality.
keratin: A nitrogenous substance, or mixture of substances, containing sulphur in a loose state of combination, and forming the chemical basis of epidermal tissues, such as horn, hair, feathers, and the like. It is an insoluble substance, and, unlike elastin, is not dissolved even by gastric or pancreatic juice.
keratosa: An order of sponges having a skeleton composed of hornlike fibers. It includes the commercial sponges.
kemp: Coarse, rough hair wool or fur, injuring its quality.
kers: A cress. (old) Chaucer. Not worth a kers. See under Cress.
key: 1. An instrument by means of which the bolt of a lock is shot or drawn; usually, a removable metal instrument fitted to the mechanism of a particular lock and operated by turning in its place. 2. | To fasten or secure firmly; to fasten or tighten with keys or wedges. Francis. To key up. (a) (Arch.) To raise (the whole ring of an arch) off its centering, by driving in the keystone forcibly.
keilhauite: A mineral of a brownish black color, related to titanite in form. It consists chiefly of silica, titanium dioxide, lime, and yttria.
kefir: An effervescent liquor like kumiss, made from fermented milk, used as a food and as a medicine in the northern Caucasus. -- Ke*fir"ic (#), a.
keelivine: A pencil of black or red lead; -- called also keelyvine pen. [Scot.] Sir W. Scott.
kernbaby: A doll or image decorated with corn (grain) flowers, etc., carried in the festivals of a kern, or harvest-home. Called also harvest queen.
kempt: p. p. of Kemb. B. Jonson.
keratonyxis: The operation of removing a cataract by thrusting a needle through the cornea of the eye, and breaking up the opaque mass.
kea: A large New Zealand parrot (Nestor notabilis), notorious for having acquired the habit of killing sheep; -- called also mountain parrot.
keraunograph: A figure or picture impressed by lightning upon the human body or elsewhere. -- Ker`au-nog"ra-phy, n.
kenning: 1. Range of sight. (old) Bacon. 2. The limit of vision at sea, being a distance of about twenty miles.
kernelly: Full of kernels; resembling kernels; of the nature of kernels. Holland.
keenness: The quality or state of being keen.
keitloa: A black, two-horned, African rhinoceros (Atelodus keitloa). It has the posterior horn about as long as the anterior one, or even longer.
kell: A sort of pottage; kale. See Kale, 2. Ainsworth. | 1. The caul; that which covers or envelops as a caul; a net; a fold; a film. (old) I'll have him cut to the kell. Beau. & Fl. 2. The cocoon or chrysalis of an insect. B. Jonson.
kemps: The long flower stems of the ribwort plantain (Plantago Lanceolata). Dr. Prior.
kephalin: One of a group of nitrogenous phosphorized principles, supposed by Thudichum to exist in brain tissue.
keyhole: 1. A hole or apertupe in a door or lock, for receiving a key. 2. (a) (Carp.) A hole or excavation in beams intended to be joined together, to receive the key which fastens them. (b) (Mach.) a mortise for a key or cotter. Keyhole limpet (Zoöl.), a marine gastropod of the genus Fissurella and allied genera. See Fissurella.
kermes: 1. (Zoöl.) The dried bodies of the females of a scale insect (Coccus ilicis), allied to the cochineal insect, and found on several species of oak near the Mediterranean. They are round, about the size of a pea, contain coloring matter analogous to carmine, and are used in dyeing. They were anciently thought to be of a vegetable nature, and were used in medicine.
kerseys: Varieties of kersey; also, trousers made of kersey.
keratome: An instrument for dividing the cornea in operations for cataract.
kelter: Regular order or proper condition. [Written also kilter.] [Colloq.] If the organs of prayer be out of kelter or out of tune, how can we pray Barrow.
keech: A mass or lump of fat rolled up by the butcher. (old) Shak.
kelpie: An imaginary spirit of the waters, horselike in form, vulgarly believed to warn, by preternatural noises and lights, those who are to be drowned. Jamieson.
keel: To cool; to akin or stir (old) While greasy Joan doth keel the pot. Shak. | A brewer's cooling vat; a keelfat.
keycold: Cold as a metallic key; lifeless. [Formerly, a proverbial expression.] Shak. Milton.
kepi: A military cap having a close-fitting band, a round flat top sloping toward the front, and a visor. As originally worn by the French in Algeria about 1830 it was tall and stiff with a straight visor. It is now lower, has a curved visor, and is frequently soft.
keelson: A piece of timber in a ship laid on the middle of the floor timbers over the keel, and binding the floor timbers to the keel; in iron vessels, a structure of plates, situated like the keelson of a timber ship. Cross keelson, a similar structure lying athwart the main keelson, to support the engines and boilers.
kettle: A metallic vessel, with a wide mouth, often without a cover, used for heating and boiling water or other liguids. Kettle pins, ninepins; skittles. (old) Shelton. -- Kettle stitch (Bookbinding), the stitch made in sewing at the head and tail of a book. Knight.
keratogenous: Producing horn; as, the keratogenous membrane within the horny hoof of the horse.
kelpy: An imaginary spirit of the waters, horselike in form, vulgarly believed to warn, by preternatural noises and lights, those who are to be drowned. Jamieson.
kenogenesis: Modified evolution, in which nonprimitive characters make their appearance in consequence of a secondary adaptation of the embryo to the peculiar conditions of its environment; -- distinguished from palingenesis. [Written also cænogenesis.]
keystone: The central or topmost stone of an arch. This in some styles is made different in size from the other voussoirs, or projects, or is decorated with carving. See Illust. of Arch. Keystone State, the State of Pennsylvania; -- so called from its having been the central State of the Union at the formation of the Constitution.
ketol: One of a series of series of complex nitrogenous substances, represented by methyl ketol and related to indol. Methyl ketol, a weak organic base, obtained as a white crystalline substance having the odor of fæces.
kecksy: The hollow stalk of an umbelliferous plant, such as the cow parsnip or the hemlock. [Written also kex, and in pl., kecks, kaxes.] Nothing teems But hateful docks, rough thistles, kecksies, burs. Shak.
keelhaul: To haul under the keel of a ship, by ropes attached to the yardarms on each side. It was formerly practiced as a punishment in the Dutch and English navies. Totten.
kerchieft: Dressed; hooded; covered; wearing a kerchief. Milton.
keckling: Old rope or iron chains wound around a cable. See Keckle, v. t.
ken: A house; esp., one which is a resort for thieves. [Slang, Eng.] | 1. To know; to understand; to take cognizance of. [Archaic or Scot.] 2. To recognize; to descry; to discern. [Archaic or Scot.] "We ken them from afar." Addison 'T is he.
keeping: 1. A holding; restraint; custody; guard; charge; care; preservation. His happiness is in his own keeping. South. 2. Maintenance; support; provision; feed; as, the cattle have good keeping. The work of many hands, which earns my keeping. Milton. 3. Conformity; congruity; harmony; consistency; as, these subjects are in keeping with each other. 4.
kentbugle: A curved bugle, having six finger keys or stops, by means of which the performer can play upon every key in the musical scale; -- called also keyed bugle, and key bugle. Moore.
keck: To heave or to retch, as in an effort to vomit. Swift. | An effort to vomit; queasiness.
keelfat: A cooler; a vat for cooling wort, etc. [Written also keelvat.] Johnson.
kerosene: An oil used for illuminating purposes, formerly obtained from the distillation of mineral wax, bituminous shale, etc., and hence called also coal oil. It is now produced in immense quantities, chiefly by the distillation and purification of petroleum. It consists chiefly of several hydrocarbons of the methane series.
kentucky: One of the United States. Kentucky blue grass (Bot.), a valuable pasture and meadow grass (Poa pratensis), found in both Europe and America. See under Blue grass. -- Kentucky coffee tree (Bot.), a tall North American tree (Gymnocladus Canadensis) with bipinnate leaves. It produces large woody pods containing a few seeds which have been used as a substitute for coffee.
ketine: One of a series of organic bases obtained by the reduction of certain isonitroso compounds of the ketones. In general they are unstable oily substances having a pungent aromatic odor.
ketmie: The name of certain African species of Hibiscus, cultivated for the acid of their mucilage. [Written also ketmia.]
kee: See Kie, Ky, and Kine. [Prov. Eng.] Gay.
kerned: Having part of the face projecting beyond the body or shank; -- said of type. "In Roman, f and j are the only kerned letters." MacKellar.
keddah: An inclosure constructed to entrap wild elephants; an elephant trap. [India]
ketonic: Pertaining to, or derived from, a ketone; as, a ketonic acid.
keratophyte: A gorgonian coral having a horny axis.
keslop: The stomach of a calf, prepared for rennet. Halliwell.
kex: 1. (Bot.) A weed; a kecksy. Bp. Gauden. Though the rough kex break The starred mosaic. Tennyson. 2. A dry husk or covering. When the kex, or husk, is broken, he proveth a fair flying butterfly. Holland.
kerasin: A nitrogenous substance free from phosphorus, supposed to be present in the brain; a body closely related to cerebrin.
kept: of Keep. Kept mistress, a concubine; a woman supported by a man as his paramour.
kettledrummer: One who plays on a kettledrum.
keramographic: Suitable to be written upon; capable of being written upon, as a slate; -- said especially of a certain kind of globe. Scudamore.
kemelin: A tub; a brewer's vessel. (old) Chaucer.
keyed: Furnished with keys; as, a keyed instrument; also, set to a key, as a tune. Keyed bugle. See Kent bugle.
keuper: The upper division of the European Triassic. See Chart of Geology.
